items.title: Teaching AI the biology of antibodies speeds drug discovery
items.excerpt: Boston University researchers built an antibody-specific language model that concentrates on the six binding loops instead of the whole protein, improving binding-strength prediction by up to 27%. Encoding domain biology into the architecture beat treating antibodies as generic proteins.

items.title: Real-time X-ray data analysis with DONUT accelerates materials science
items.excerpt: Argonne National Laboratory built DONUT, a physics-aware machine learning tool that interprets X-ray diffraction data hundreds of times faster than conventional analysis. Scientists can now steer experiments while they run, a building block for autonomous, self-driving materials labs.

items.title: Rivers are moving sediment in intense bursts, a worrisome new pattern uncovered by AI
items.excerpt: Virginia Tech researchers ran AI over 40 years of sediment records from 175 U.S. rivers and found rivers now pack 90% of annual sediment transport into about 50 days, down from 69. The compression, driven by urbanization and forest loss, threatens drinking-water systems and aquatic ecosystems.

items.title: Empty shelves or lost keys? Recall is the bottleneck for parametric factuality
items.excerpt: Google Research's 'knowledge profiling' framework shows frontier LLMs encode 95–98% of tested facts yet still fail to recall 26–34% of them. The failure mode is retrieval, not missing knowledge — a direct reframing of why models hallucinate.

items.title: TutorMoments: Do AI tutors know when to help and when to hold back?
items.excerpt: Ai2 released a framework that measures whether language models can judge when to support a student versus when to let them struggle productively. Models systematically over-help unless the pedagogical trade-off is spelled out in the prompt.

items.title: New AI technique helps robots complete tasks twice as fast by letting them 'think ahead'
items.excerpt: Researchers built VLASH, a system that lets a robot plan its next action while still executing the current one, cutting reaction delay up to 11.8x and roughly doubling task completion speed. The gain comes with no extra compute overhead.

items.title: New AI chip mimics the human brain's capacity for split-second motor control
items.excerpt: A neuromorphic chip modeled on the brain's fast motor-control circuitry solved control problems with roughly 10,000 times fewer calculations than conventional approaches. It is a concrete case of brain-inspired architecture beating brute-force compute.

items.title: Human biological datacenter to launch to train world model of human biology
items.excerpt: Vivodyne is opening what it calls the world's largest human biological datacenter: 12 robotic labs running 3.1 million lab-grown human tissue trials a year. The output is training data for an AI world model spanning 22 organ systems.

items.title: How kids feel about AI, in their own words
items.excerpt: MIT Technology Review surveyed 10–18-year-olds and found they treat AI as an ordinary utility for schoolwork and search rather than a revolution, worrying more about society than their own future jobs. Pew data backs the pattern: 57% use chatbots to look things up, only 12% for emotional support.

items.title: No, Anthropic's AI didn't just solve math's hardest problem
items.excerpt: Claude did push a real result on the distribution of zeta zeros from 41.6% to 67.2%, but the Riemann hypothesis itself is untouched. The piece is a case study in how AI math claims get inflated between the proof and the press release.

items.title: Science YouTuber Hank Green used AI to research his videos. His fans pushed back
items.excerpt: Hank Green's disclosure that he leaned on ChatGPT for video research triggered a backlash from his own audience. The fight is about where AI sits in the research-and-verify chain of science communication, and how much trust disclosure actually buys.

items.title: Is AI Reasoning Right for the Wrong Reasons?
items.excerpt: Quanta walks through the conflicting evidence on whether large reasoning models actually reason or just pattern-match their way to correct answers. Melanie Mitchell and Subbarao Kambhampati argue the visible 'thinking tokens' may not faithfully describe what the model is doing.

items.title: AI sniffs out tuberculosis in breath's chemical signature
items.excerpt: A team at Botswana International University of Science and Technology used support vector machines on volatile organic compounds in exhaled breath to detect tuberculosis with 93% accuracy. The method works on raw signatures without aggressive data filtering, pointing to low-cost screening.

items.title: Nurses seek a seat at the table as they fight expanding clinical AI
items.excerpt: Nurses, the largest slice of the healthcare workforce, are pushing to be part of how clinical AI gets designed and deployed rather than having it land on them. The demand: turn tool-versus-worker conflict into co-design of the workflow.

items.title: Putting sign language AI into users' hands
items.excerpt: DeepMind shipped SL2T, a massively multilingual sign-language-to-text translation model trained on 100,000+ hours across 50+ sign languages, into Gboard and Live Transcribe on Pixel 11. It is the first consumer deployment of sign-language translation research.

items.title: AI Therapists Are Coming (for the Next Generation)
items.excerpt: A 2026 YouGov survey finds 66% of Americans are uncomfortable with AI therapy, but under-30s are twice as likely as older adults to accept it (37% vs 20%). The generational split suggests the acceptance curve, not the technology, is the gating factor.

items.title: How Your Children View AI and Why It Matters
items.excerpt: A study of 521 4th and 8th graders in Türkiye mapped children's mental representations of AI: older and heavier device users hold more abstract, complex models, while girls describe AI in emotional and social terms and boys in technical ones. Early mental models shape lifelong trust calibration.
